newsitem.title: UK: Delta sees more changes for Europe.
newsitem.headline: Delta sees more changes for Europe.

text.p: U.S. carrier Delta Air Lines said the overhaul of its transatlantic and European network which it announced on Tuesday would be followed shortly by a relaunch of its transatlantic premium class services.
Delta's vice president for Europe and Asia Michael Medlicott told a news conference in London the airline hoped to be able to make an announcement "in another four or five weeks."

Medlicott also said although the changes announced earlier would strengthen its own alliances in mainland Europe it would be pressing ahead with its opposition to the proposed tie-up between British Airways and American Airlines.

He said most of the changes announced earlier were largely to do with mainland Europe and Delta would be making further representations to the British competition authorities about the BA/American deal later this week.

Last month Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) asked other airlines to submit comments by January 10 on British trade minister Ian Lang's proposals to approve the deal provided that BA and American release a total of 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport to make space for more competition.

Medlicott declined to detail what Delta would be telling the OFT this week but said the airline's general position was that the concessions did not go far enough to allow other airlines to establish "meaningful competition" at Heathrow.

He said if Britain went ahead and approved the deal then Delta would take the fight to the U.S. where BA and American still have to negotiate a series of regulatory obstacles laid down by the U.S. departments of Justice and Transportation.
"The conditions placed on it (British approval) are way too few," he said. " I am quite confident that Washington will be a good deal more demanding in (making its) conditions," he said.

Washington is linking approval to getting an "open skies" air services agreement with Britain which would entail giving all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow, regarded as Europe's most popular and lucrative hub for transatlantic air traffic.
Under the current bilateral trade agreement only four airlines, American, United Airlines, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic are allowed to operate transatlantic services out of Heathrow.
Medlicott said that if Delta secured access to Heathrow it would not mean the end of a deal it has with Virgin to links Delta's U.S. network with Virgin's services.
But the current annual agreement whereby Delta buys wholesale blocks of seats on Virgin's flights would change.
"We would need to rationalise our services and look hard at who does what...but in no sense would it necessarily spell the end of the relationship," Medlicott said.
Delta and Virgin said the present agreement which dates back to April 1995 is subject to annual renegotiation.
